t: The lines were made between 500 BCE and 500 CE, in a Paracas phase (400 to 200 BCE) and a Nazca phase (200 BCE to 500 CE), by removing the reddish-brown pebbles of the desert surface to show the lighter subsoil.

Scholars differ over their purpose but in general ascribe religious significance to them; astronomical, water-related, ceremonial and calendrical explanations have each been argued, while the idea of ancient astronauts has been refuted.
Drones and machine learning have raised the number of known figures from a few dozen to hundreds in the 21st century, and archaeologists expect more to be found.
dyk: Joe Nickell reproduced the figures in the early 21st century with tools of the kind the Nazca people had, and found that a small team could recreate even the largest figures within days, without aerial assistance.
ev: Earliest date given for the making of the lines, which continued until about 500 CE in a Paracas and a Nazca phase
Pedro Cieza de León published the first mention of the lines, describing them as trail markers
Toribio Mejía Xesspe spotted the lines while hiking through the foothills
Paul Kosok, in Peru to study irrigation systems, flew over the lines and recognised a bird among them
UNESCO designated the area a World Heritage Site
Yamagata University and IBM Japan announced 143 new geoglyphs, one of them found by machine learning
Archaeologists from Yamagata University's Nazca Institute and IBM Research used artificial intelligence to find 303 previously unknown figurative geoglyphs

f.made: The people of the Paracas and Nazca phases, between 500 BCE and 500 CE, working with simple tools and surveying equipment
f.form: Geoglyphs made by shallow trenches 10 to 15 cm deep in the desert floor: straight lines, geometric shapes and more than 70 zoomorphic designs, the largest about 370 m long, with a combined length of more than 1,300 km
f.where: The Nazca Desert on the Pampas de Jumana, a high plateau of southern Peru between the towns of Nazca and Palpa, about 400 km south of Lima
f.known: huge animal and plant figures, among them a hummingbird, spider, condor and monkey; long straight lines; designs best seen from the air; debated purposes from astronomy to water rituals; new figures found by drones and machine learning; a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1994
